clinicalPearls: The most common congenital midline neck cyst in children, usually presenting as a painless swelling near or just below the hyoid bone
A characteristic sign is that the lump moves upward on swallowing and on protrusion of the tongue, reflecting its attachment to the tract from the foramen caecum
It arises from remnants of the thyroglossal duct along the path of embryological descent of the thyroid gland
Cysts may present acutely when they become infected, appearing as a tender, red, sometimes discharging midline mass
Before excision it is important to confirm the presence of normally located thyroid tissue, because rarely the cyst contains the only functioning thyroid (ectopic thyroid)
Ultrasound is the preferred first investigation and helps confirm normal thyroid gland location
Definitive treatment is the Sistrunk operation, which removes the cyst together with the central portion of the hyoid bone and the tract up to the tongue base to minimise recurrence
Simple incision or local excision without removing the tract and mid-hyoid leads to high recurrence rates
reference.pathophysiology: During development the thyroid gland descends from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to its final pretracheal position, leaving behind the thyroglossal duct, which normally involutes. Persistence of epithelial remnants along this tract allows a fluid-filled cyst to form anywhere from the tongue base to the thyroid, but most commonly at or near the hyoid bone. Its intimate relationship with the hyoid explains the movement with swallowing and tongue protrusion, and retained secretions or infection cause enlargement and inflammation.
additionalDifferentials: Dermoid cyst of the midline neck
Branchial or other lateral neck cyst (if off midline)
additionalInvestigations: Neck ultrasound to characterise the cyst and confirm a normally sited thyroid gland
Thyroid function tests where ectopic thyroid is a concern
Cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) in atypical, recurrent, or deep lesions
Fine-needle aspiration reserved for suspicious or atypical masses
Radionuclide thyroid scan if ectopic functioning tissue must be confirmed
redFlags: Acute infection with abscess formation requiring drainage and antibiotic treatment
A solid or rapidly enlarging component, or the presence of a suspicious nodule, raising the rare possibility of malignancy
Evidence that the cyst represents the only functioning thyroid tissue, which contraindicates simple excision
Airway compromise from a large lingual or tongue-base lesion
reference.prognosis: Following a properly performed Sistrunk procedure the outlook is excellent with low recurrence. Recurrence is more likely after inadequate surgery or when a preceding infection has distorted the tissue planes, and malignant change within the cyst is rare.
pitfalls: Excising the cyst alone without the mid-hyoid and tract, leading to recurrence
Operating without first confirming a normally located, functioning thyroid gland
Attempting definitive surgery during acute infection rather than controlling infection first
Mistaking a midline dermoid or ectopic thyroid for a simple thyroglossal cyst
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Definitive treatment is the Sistrunk procedure, excising the cyst, its tract and the central portion of the hyoid, which minimises recurrence
Confirm a normally sited, functioning orthotopic thyroid gland on ultrasound before excision, since the cyst rarely contains the only functioning thyroid tissue
Treat acute infection with antibiotics and drainage of any abscess, allowing inflammation to settle before definitive surgery
Assess thyroid function and provide thyroxine replacement if the orthotopic thyroid is ectopic or absent
Submit the excised specimen for histology given the rare possibility of malignant change
Refer to paediatric surgery or otolaryngology for planned excision
